## Swarm Mode

You are now in "agent swarm" mode. The user may send tasks that require a large number of parallel subagents.

## Workflow

You do not need to use TodoList to record this workflow.

1. First, you may need to do a small amount of exploratory work before deciding how to divide the task across subagents. You may not need subagents during this exploratory phase.

2. After exploring, if you are convinced no subagent is needed to complete the task, tell the user why and wait for further instructions; otherwise, continue with the appropriate delegation.

3. Once you have enough context, do not handle the main work yourself. Use AgentSwarm with a `prompt_template` containing the `{{item}}` placeholder and an `items` array for the requested or appropriate number of subagents, partitioning the problem so each item gives one subagent a distinct part of the work. Pass `subagent_type` when the whole swarm should use a non-default subagent profile.

## Coordination

- Give each subagent a distinct scope of work.
- Avoid duplicating work across subagents.
- Avoid assigning conflicting changes or responsibilities to different subagents.
- Remember that subagents have your full capabilities. Do not overload their prompts with excessive detail; only describe the necessary background and each subagent's specific task.
- Unless the user explicitly specifies a lower limit, do not try to conserve the number of agents. AgentSwarm supports up to 128 subagents and queues launches automatically, so decompose work as finely as possible while keeping subagent responsibilities non-conflicting; combine tasks only when they are genuinely inseparable. If the subagents only need to read, inspect, or report back without making changes, their scopes may overlap slightly.
</system-reminder>

You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this - finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool - does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only - your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

1	# RustOwl Configuration (Neovim)
2	
3	This document describes all available configuration options for the RustOwl Neovim plugin.
4	
5	## Table of Contents
6	
7	- [Basic Setup](#basic-setup)
8	- [Configuration Options](#configuration-options)
9	- [Customizing Highlight Colors](#customizing-highlight-colors)
10	- [Examples](#examples)
11	
12	## Basic Setup
13	
14	The minimal configuration for RustOwl using [lazy.nvim](https://github.com/folke/lazy.nvim):
15	
16	```lua
17	{
18	  'cordx56/rustowl',
19	  version = '*', -- Latest stable version
20	  build = 'cargo binstall rustowl',
21	  lazy = false, -- This plugin is already lazy
22	  opts = {},
23	}
24	```
25	
26	## Configuration Options
27	
28	All configuration options are optional and have sensible defaults:
29	
30	### `auto_attach` (boolean)
31	
32	- **Default**: `true`
33	- **Description**: Automatically attach the RustOwl LSP client when opening a Rust file.
34	
35	### `auto_enable` (boolean)
36	
37	- **Default**: `false`
38	- **Description**: Enable RustOwl highlighting immediately when the LSP client attaches. When `false`, you need to manually enable highlighting using `:Rustowl enable` or `require('rustowl').enable()`.
39	
40	### `idle_time` (number)
41	
42	- **Default**: `500`
43	- **Description**: Time in milliseconds to hover with the cursor before triggering RustOwl analysis and highlighting.
44	
45	### `highlight_style` (string)
46	
47	- **Default**: `'undercurl'`
48	- **Options**: `'undercurl'` or `'underline'`
49	- **Description**: The style of underline to use for highlighting.
50	
51	### `colors` (table)
52	
53	- **Description**: Custom colors for different highlight types. Each color should be a hex color string (e.g., `'#ff0000'`).
54	
55	#### Available Color Options:
56	
57	- `lifetime`: Color for variable lifetime highlights (default: `'#00cc00'` - green)
58	- `imm_borrow`: Color for immutable borrow highlights (default: `'#0000cc'` - blue)
59	- `mut_borrow`: Color for mutable borrow highlights (default: `'#cc00cc'` - purple)
60	- `move`: Color for value move highlights (default: `'#cccc00'` - yellow)
61	- `call`: Color for function call highlights (default: `'#cccc00'` - yellow)
62	- `outlive`: Color for lifetime error highlights (default: `'#cc0000'` - red)
63	
64	### `client` (table)
65	
66	- **Description**: LSP client configuration that gets passed to `vim.lsp.start`. This follows the same structure as Neovim's LSP client configuration.
67	
68	## Customizing Highlight Colors
69	
70	### Default Colors
71	
72	The default color scheme uses the following colors that correspond to the visual legend:
73	
74	- 🟩 **Green** (`#00cc00`): Variable's actual lifetime
75	- 🟦 **Blue** (`#0000cc`): Immutable borrowing
76	- 🟪 **Purple** (`#cc00cc`): Mutable borrowing
77	- 🟧 **Yellow** (`#cccc00`): Value moved / function call
78	- 🟥 **Red** (`#cc0000`): Lifetime errors
79	
80	### Custom Colors
81	
82	To customize colors, specify them in the `colors` table:
83	
84	```lua
85	opts = {
86	  colors = {
87	    lifetime = '#32cd32',   -- Lime green
88	    imm_borrow = '#4169e1', -- Royal blue
89	    mut_borrow = '#ff69b4', -- Hot pink
90	    move = '#ffa500',       -- Orange
91	    call = '#ffd700',       -- Gold
92	    outlive = '#dc143c',    -- Crimson
93	  },
94	}
95	```
96	
97	#### Color Format
98	
99	Colors must be specified as hex color strings:
100	
101	- ✅ Valid: `'#ff0000'`, `'#00ff00'`, `'#0000ff'`
102	- ❌ Invalid: `'red'`, `'rgb(255,0,0)'`, `'#f00'`
103	
104	### Partial Color Customization
105	
106	You can customize only specific colors while keeping the defaults for others:
107	
108	```lua
109	opts = {
110	  colors = {
111	    lifetime = '#90ee90',   -- Light green for better visibility
112	    outlive = '#ff4500',    -- Orange red for errors
113	    -- Other colors will use defaults
114	  },
115	}
116	```
117	
118	## Examples
119	
120	### Example 1: Minimal Configuration
121	
122	```lua
123	{
124	  'cordx56/rustowl',
125	  version = '*',
126	  build = 'cargo binstall rustowl',
127	  lazy = false,
128	  opts = {},
129	}
130	```
131	
132	### Example 2: Auto-enable with Custom Colors
133	
134	```lua
135	{
136	  'cordx56/rustowl',
137	  version = '*',
138	  build = 'cargo binstall rustowl',
139	  lazy = false,
140	  opts = {
141	    auto_enable = true,
142	    colors = {
143	      lifetime = '#90ee90',   -- Light green
144	      imm_borrow = '#87ceeb', -- Sky blue
145	      mut_borrow = '#dda0dd', -- Plum
146	      move = '#f0e68c',       -- Khaki
147	      call = '#ffd700',       -- Gold
148	      outlive = '#ff6347',    -- Tomato
149	    },
150	  },
151	}
152	```
153	
154	### Example 3: Custom Key Binding and Styling
155	
156	```lua
157	{
158	  'cordx56/rustowl',
159	  version = '*',
160	  build = 'cargo binstall rustowl',
161	  lazy = false,
162	  opts = {
163	    auto_enable = false,
164	    idle_time = 300,
165	    highlight_style = 'underline',
166	    colors = {
167	      outlive = '#ff0000', -- Bright red for errors
168	    },
169	    client = {
170	      on_attach = function(_, buffer)
171	        vim.keymap.set('n', '<leader>ro', function()
172	          require('rustowl').toggle(buffer)
173	        end, { buffer = buffer, desc = 'Toggle RustOwl' })
174	
175	        vim.keymap.set('n', '<leader>re', function()
176	          require('rustowl').enable(buffer)
177	        end, { buffer = buffer, desc = 'Enable RustOwl' })
178	
179	        vim.keymap.set('n', '<leader>rd', function()
180	          require('rustowl').disable(buffer)
181	        end, { buffer = buffer, desc = 'Disable RustOwl' })
182	      end
183	    },
184	  },
185	}
186	```
187	
188	### Example 4: Dark Theme Optimized Colors
189	
190	```lua
191	{
192	  'cordx56/rustowl',
193	  version = '*',
194	  build = 'cargo binstall rustowl',
195	  lazy = false,
196	  opts = {
197	    colors = {
198	      lifetime = '#50fa7b',   -- Dracula green
199	      imm_borrow = '#8be9fd', -- Dracula cyan
200	      mut_borrow = '#ff79c6', -- Dracula pink
201	      move = '#f1fa8c',       -- Dracula yellow
202	      call = '#ffb86c',       -- Dracula orange
203	      outlive = '#ff5555',    -- Dracula red
204	    },
205	  },
206	}
207	```
208	
209	### Example 5: For init.vim Users
210	
211	If you're using `init.vim` instead of `init.lua`, you can configure RustOwl using Vim script:
212	
213	```vim
214	lua << EOF
215	require('lazy').setup({
216	  {
217	    'cordx56/rustowl',
218	    version = '*',
219	    build = 'cargo binstall rustowl',
220	    lazy = false,
221	    opts = {
222	      colors = {
223	        lifetime = '#00ff00',
224	        imm_borrow = '#0080ff',
225	        mut_borrow = '#ff00ff',
226	        move = '#ffff00',
227	        call = '#ffa500',
228	        outlive = '#ff0000',
229	      },
230	    },
231	  },
232	})
233	EOF
234	```
235	
236	## Usage Commands
237	
238	When opening a Rust file, the following commands become available:
239	
240	- `:Rustowl start_client` - Start the RustOwl LSP client
241	- `:Rustowl stop_client` - Stop the RustOwl LSP client
242	- `:Rustowl restart_client` - Restart the RustOwl LSP client
243	- `:Rustowl enable` - Enable RustOwl highlighting
244	- `:Rustowl disable` - Disable RustOwl highlighting
245	- `:Rustowl toggle` - Toggle RustOwl highlighting
246	
247	You can also use the Lua API:
248	
249	```lua
250	require('rustowl').enable()   -- Enable highlighting
251	require('rustowl').disable()  -- Disable highlighting
252	require('rustowl').toggle()   -- Toggle highlighting
253	require('rustowl').is_enabled() -- Check if enabled
254	```
